Eggs of the North Atlantic loggerhead turtle (Caretta caretta) contain a substantial initial energy content of 210,000 Joules , which reflects the considerable investment required to sustain embryonic development within the leathery-shelled egg. This yolk-laden resource fuels the embryo throughout incubation, with reported values ranging from 165 to 260 kJ depending on maternal condition and geographic origin. The parchment-shelled egg is deposited in a nest cavity excavated by the nesting female, where thermal conditions at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] dictate the timing of the hatching event, with eclosion occurring after approximately 51.3 days . This duration, derived from subtracting the 4.1-day interval between shell pipping and nest emergence from the total age at emergence, is consistent with incubation periods observed across the nesting range. The interval between chorion rupture and the hatchling's emergence from the nest is a critical period during which the young reptile relies on endogenous yolk reserves before initiating the crawl to the surface.

Following emergence from the nest, the neonate undergoes a brief period of yolk-sac absorption before becoming an exotrophic juvenile. The straight carapace length (SCL) at hatching is 4.5 cm , a dimension that is essentially identical to the SCL at birth of 4.5 cm [Lb = 4.5 cm], indicating minimal somatic growth during the short interval between eclosion and emergence. The yolk-free wet weight at hatching has been measured at 18.67 grams , reflecting the mass of the individual after accounting for the energy-rich yolk that sustains the lecithotrophic larva during the initial days post-hatching. However, by the time the hatchling reaches the sea surface and begins the transition to exogenous feeding, wet weight at birth increases slightly to 19.41 grams [Wwb = 19.41 grams], a change attributed to water ingestion and the onset of feeding behavior.

Juvenile loggerheads undergo a prolonged period of growth in oceanic and neritic habitats, gradually approaching the size at which reproductive maturity is attained. Field studies indicate that puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal activation, occurs when individuals reach a straight carapace length of 80 cm [Lp = 80 cm]. This threshold body size, derived from the minimum dimensions reported for gravid females in several comprehensive surveys, serves as a reliable proxy for the transition from the juvenile to the sexually mature adult stage. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 79 kilograms [Wwp = approximately 79 kilograms], a substantial body mass that reflects years of sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates such as crabs and mollusks. The age at which this size is reached, approximately 18 years after emergence [tp = approximately 18 years after emergence], is based on growth ring analysis and mark-recapture data, with the caveat that thermal conditions, particularly a mean water temperature of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C], strongly influence growth rates across the species' range.

Reproductive activity in adult females is characterized by a distinct nesting cycle that integrates multiple clutches within a single breeding season. At a mean water temperature of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C], a female typically lays 4 nests per nesting season [F_R_i = 4 nests per nesting season], with each clutch containing approximately 140 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing approximately 140 eggs]. Given the biennial interval between successive nesting seasons, which averages 2 years [F_R_i = nesting seasons, which averages 2 years], the annual reproductive output is considerable. This pattern of 5 clutches every 2.5 years yields an equivalent daily deposition rate, though field biologists typically report the frequency in terms of nesting events per season rather than as a daily average. The ultimate straight carapace length for the species has been recorded at 105.26 cm [Li = 105.26 cm], representing the mean of maximum SCL values reported across multiple long-term studies in the North Atlantic, while the ultimate wet weight reaches 162,620 grams [Wwi = 162,620 grams], corresponding to the largest individuals ever documented in the region.

The complete life cycle of the North Atlantic loggerhead spans several decades, with maximum recorded longevity estimated at 67 years [am = 67 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C]. This impressive lifespan, occurring at a mean water temperature of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C], positions Caretta caretta among the longer-lived sea turtle species, a trait linked to its slow maturation, delayed reproduction, and low adult mortality in the absence of anthropogenic threats. The age at birth, encompassing the full period from oviposition to nest emergence, is approximately 57.4 days [ab = approximately 57.4 days] when eggs are incubated at a mean nest temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], a figure that includes both the embryonation period and the yolk-sac absorption phase following eclosion. Comparative studies with congeneric species suggest that these thermal dependencies in developmental timing are highly conserved within the family Cheloniidae, with slight variations attributable to latitudinal differences in nest microclimate and maternal nest-site selection behavior.
